summary.text: 字 is traditionally explained as a child (子) beneath a roof (宀); 子 is also said to provide its sound. An early lexicographic account associates the character with birth or nurture, while its common present meaning is “written character.”

formation.text: The traditional analysis is phonosemantic: 宀 depicts a roof or indoor setting, while 子 depicts a child and is assigned a sound role. This child-under-a-roof construction is an old explanation of the graph, though the available account notes that it has been challenged without detailing the alternatives.

components.text: In the traditional interpretation, 宀 depicts a roof or indoor setting around the child. This is a proposed reading of the graph, not a settled paleographic conclusion.
In the traditional interpretation, 子 depicts the child beneath the roof and also provides a sound cue.

sound_limitation.text: The reported Old Chinese comparison is compatible with a sound role, but the exact dataset entries were not independently verified against the upstream dataset. The modern Mandarin pair alone does not establish the ancient relation.

sound.text: The reported Old Chinese forms have compatible consonant correspondences, though this comparison alone does not prove the graphic analysis.
In modern Mandarin, the readings are 子 zǐ and 字 zì; this comparison does not establish the ancient relation.

history.text: A bronze-form account describes 子 below 宀. A catalog lists a Shang-period rubbing associated with 字父己觶; that listing does not establish the inscription’s contextual reading or make it the earliest attestation.
The traditional construction has been challenged, but the available report does not detail the alternative analyses. No evidence here identifies graphic corruption or miscopying.

uncertainties.text: The child-under-a-roof construction is a transmitted historical explanation; the reported disagreement cannot be evaluated in detail from the available account.

senses.period: Han lexicographic account; earlier dating unresolved
senses.text: A Han lexicographic account gives birth or nurture as a meaning, but does not show when either sense arose or whether the glosses represent one original meaning.
字 commonly means a written character. The earliest use of this sense is not dated here.
“Word” is also a recorded meaning; its chronology and relation to birth or nurture are unresolved.

developments.text: A later commentary links birth to nurture and then to written characters; another account allows a distinct root or a derivation from producing or generating. The proposed relationship and its chronology remain unresolved.

limitations.text: Dictionary glosses and the Han-era explanation that written forms multiply do not independently establish the chronology or development of these meanings.
